title: Writing an estimate
purpose: Step two of the inspection-to-approval procedure: turning inspection findings into an estimate.
facts: The requested job first; every Bad line becomes a catalogue job; Watch lines go in the notes with the measurement, except when they share labour with a Bad item.
Prices come from the price list only; service pages can be out of date (the rule slot 7 broke, S8).
Standard tier by default; vehicle class multipliers; ordering by safety, breakdown risk, cost of delay.
The total is read with tax.
Parts availability checked with slot 9 before any time is mentioned.
Estimates over 1,000 USD get a second look from the lead advisor.

list_items.item: Start with what the customer came for. That job first, even if the inspection found something bigger.
Every Bad line becomes a job on the estimate. Pick it from the catalogue. If the technician typed a job by hand that is in the catalogue, change it to the catalogue job.

Watch lines do not go on the estimate as jobs. They go in the notes with the measurement, so the customer sees them and we find them next visit. Exception: a Watch item that shares labour with a Bad one. Say so: "while we are in there".

Price from the price list. Nowhere else. Not from memory, not from the last invoice, and not from a service page: those explain the job, and they can be out of date. The shop system prices a catalogue job for you; check it against the list if it looks odd.
Standard tier unless the customer asked otherwise. Have the economy and premium figures ready; do not lead with them.
Vehicle class. A pickup or a van is not a car: multipliers.
Order the jobs by what matters: safety, then what will strand them, then what will cost more if left, then the rest.
Shop supplies and tax are added by the system. Read the customer the total with tax, because that is what they pay.
Parts: ask Marcus whether they are on the shelf or on a run before you talk about time.
Send it the same working day. Then get the approval.

new_facts: The 1,000 USD second-look rule (habit, no data footprint).
